source_document: Document 8 - John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, 1845 (adapted)
source_text: . . . other nations have undertaken to intrude themselves into it [the question of Texas], between us and the proper parties to the case, in a spirit of hostile interference against us, for the avowed [openly stated] object of thwarting [blocking] our policy and hampering our power, limiting our greatness and checking the fulfillment of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence [God] for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions. . . .
context_line: In 1845, Texas was about to join the United States. A New York magazine argued for it.
_pointer: Teaching American History, 'Annexation' (United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July–August 1845; unsigned, attributed to O'Sullivan), checked 2026-10-15. Cut to the sentence's second half; glosses ours.
prompt: Name the principle this document is about, then say whether it upholds it, denies it, or fights over it -- point to the words that show it.
checklist: Names the principle by its card name
Says whether the document upholds it, denies it, or fights over it
Points to the words that show it
model_response: Document 8 upholds Natural Rights, but stretches it past what the card means: the card's Natural Rights belongs to a person -- life, liberty, property -- not a nation. O'Sullivan borrows its language anyway, treating America's spread across the continent as something “allotted by Providence” -- a right that comes before any government's agreement -- to make a land claim sound like something government is bound to respect. It isn't a person's right he's describing. It's a borrowed phrase doing a different job.
